concepts.title: The error Interface and Values, Not Exceptions
concepts.description: Go represents failure as an ordinary value satisfying a one-method interface, and callers are expected to check it explicitly right after the call that might have produced it -- understanding why this design was chosen over exceptions is the foundation for everything else about error handling in Go.
learningObjectives: Define the error interface and explain why any type with an Error() string method satisfies it.
Explain the idiomatic `if err != nil` pattern and why Go returns errors as ordinary values instead of using exceptions.
Construct errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf, and explain when to reach for each.
Define a sentinel error and use == to check for it.
Explain why ignoring a returned error (assigning it to _) compiles without complaint, and why that's dangerous.
Predict the behavior of code that uses a function's result value before checking whether it also returned a non-nil error.

sections.heading: The error Interface: One Method, No Exceptions
Constructing Errors: errors.New and fmt.Errorf
Sentinel Errors: Checking for a Specific, Known Failure
The Zero-Value-Plus-Error Convention -- and the Mistake of Using the Result Too Early
Why Go Rejected Exceptions for Ordinary Failures
sections.body:
It's worth being explicit about the design rationale, because it explains choices you'll see throughout the standard library and any well-written Go codebase. Exceptions, in languages that have them, are usually used for two very different kinds of situations at once: routine, expected failures (a file doesn't exist, a network request times out, user input is malformed) and genuinely exceptional, program-breaking situations (an invariant your own code assumed was impossible has been violated). Go draws a hard line between these two: **ordinary, expected failures are represented as `error` return values that the caller is expected to check and handle inline; only truly exceptional situations use `panic`**, a separate mechanism covered later in this module, and even then only sparingly.

The trade-off is real and worth naming honestly: this makes Go code visibly more repetitive than the equivalent in a language leaning on exceptions, where a dozen calls that could each fail can sit inside one `try` block with a single `catch` handling all of them at once. Go's answer is that this repetition buys something valuable in return -- every failure path is visible, local, and impossible to accidentally skip past without the compiler at least forcing you to have received the error value in the first place (even if, as the next section covers, you can still choose to discard it). A reader scanning a Go function top to bottom can see every single point where it might fail and exactly what happens at each one, without needing to also mentally simulate which lines could throw and trace where control would jump to if they did.

examples.title: Using a Result Before Checking Its Error
examples.explanation: `strconv.Atoi("not-a-number")` fails, returning `0` (int's zero value) alongside a non-nil error describing the parse failure. Nothing here panics or crashes -- `value` is a completely ordinary, usable `0`. The bug is that `doubled := value * 2` runs before the code ever checks `err`, so it silently computes and prints `doubled: 0`, a number that looks like legitimate output but is actually meaningless, derived from a failed parse. The error message does eventually print, but by then the wrong computed value has already been used (and here, printed) as if it were real. The fix is purely about ordering: check `err` immediately after the call that produced it, and only use `value` in the branch where `err == nil`.

examples.title: A Sentinel Error Compared with ==
examples.explanation: `Pop` always returns the exact same `ErrEmptyQueue` value -- the one created once at package scope -- whenever the queue is empty, rather than constructing a new error with matching text each time. That's what makes `err == ErrEmptyQueue` a reliable check: both sides of the comparison are the literal same value in memory, not merely two errors that happen to render the same message. If `Pop` had instead written `return 0, errors.New("queue is empty")` inline, the comparison `err == ErrEmptyQueue` would be false every single time, even though the text matches exactly -- `errors.New` allocates a distinct value on every call, and `==` on interface values compares identity/underlying value, not string contents.

examples.title: Silently Discarding an Error with the Blank Identifier
examples.explanation: `os.ReadFile` returns `([]byte, error)`; assigning the error to `_` compiles perfectly cleanly -- Go's unused-variable rule only fires for named variables that are declared and never read, and `_` is specifically the blank identifier, exempt from that rule by design, precisely so you *can* deliberately ignore a value you don't care about. The trouble is that here, the error genuinely does matter: if `config.json` doesn't exist or can't be read, `data` is `nil` (the zero value for a byte slice), and `string(data)` is simply the empty string -- so the program prints `config contents: ` with nothing after it and continues running as if it had successfully loaded an empty (rather than missing) config file. No crash, no visible symptom at this exact line -- the bug surfaces later, disguised as 'the config seems empty' rather than 'the config failed to load,' which is a much harder problem to trace back to its actual cause.

misconceptions.description: Since Go doesn't have exceptions, a function call that fails will always cause the program to stop or crash right at that point, similar to an unhandled exception.
misconceptions.clarification: Nothing crashes automatically. An `error` is just an ordinary value sitting in a return slot -- if you never check it (or explicitly discard it with `_`), the program keeps running normally, using whatever zero value or partial result came back alongside that ignored error, with no warning at all. This is arguably more dangerous than a language that crashes loudly on unhandled failures, precisely because an ignored Go error produces no visible symptom at the failure site -- the bug surfaces later, often far from its actual cause, as corrupted or missing data rather than a clear crash with a stack trace pointing at the real problem.

misconceptions.description: Two error values built from the same message text, such as two separate calls to errors.New("not found"), are equal when compared with ==.
misconceptions.clarification: `errors.New` allocates and returns a distinct value on every single call, even when given identical text -- comparing two independently-constructed errors with `==` is false, regardless of whether their `Error()` strings happen to match exactly. The sentinel-error pattern works specifically because a package stores one error value once, in a package-level variable, and every code path that wants to signal that specific failure returns that same stored value rather than constructing a fresh one -- `==` then correctly recognizes the same value coming back, but it is never comparing message strings under the hood.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why doesn't it crash even though the conversion fails?
hints: strconv.Atoi returns (int, error) -- what does it return for the int when parsing fails, rather than leaving it undefined?
Recall Go's zero-value guarantee: a failed operation that returns an int alongside a non-nil error still returns a completely valid, safe int -- just the type's zero value.
Nothing here panics, because err is a normal returned value, not a thrown exception -- the program simply continues to the next line, which prints both results exactly as returned.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'age: 0' and then 'err: strconv.Atoi: parsing "abc": invalid syntax' (or a very similarly worded message). Atoi returns int's zero value, 0, alongside a descriptive non-nil error when parsing fails -- there's no crash because a returned error is just an ordinary value, not a thrown exception that could halt execution on its own.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `strconv.Atoi("abc")` cannot parse "abc" as an integer, so it returns two things: `0` (the zero value for `int`, per Go's zero-value guarantee) and a non-nil `error` describing exactly what went wrong. Because Go errors are ordinary values rather than exceptions, nothing about this failure interrupts control flow -- execution proceeds straight to the next line regardless of whether `err` is nil or not. Both `fmt.Println` calls run normally, printing whatever `age` and `err` actually hold: `0` and the descriptive parse-failure message, respectively. If this code had gone on to *use* `age` as if the parse had succeeded (say, multiplying it by a price), it would have silently computed a nonsense result from the meaningless zero value -- exactly the kind of bug that motivates checking `err` immediately after the call.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to read a config file and report clearly when it's missing, but a caller who forgets to check the returned error ends up treating a missing config as if it were successfully loaded with empty contents. Find the ordering bug and fix it so acting on the data is impossible unless the read actually succeeded.
hints: Look at the order of operations inside loadConfig: is `data` used (via len(data)) before or after err is actually checked?
Even though the function does eventually check err and print a warning, it already used and returned data regardless of what that check found.
The fix should check err first and return early -- with an empty string and no further use of data -- before doing anything else with data, including printing its length.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code calls `len(data)` and later `return string(data)` regardless of whether the read actually succeeded -- checking `err` only ever produced an extra warning printed alongside the (wrong) result, it never changed what got returned. Since a failed `os.ReadFile` returns `nil` for `data` (the zero value for `[]byte`), `len(data)` is `0` and `string(data)` is `""`, so the caller receives an empty string indistinguishable from 'the file genuinely exists and is empty.' The fix moves the `err != nil` check to immediately after the call and returns early with `""` in that branch, before `data` is used for anything else at all -- this guarantees the rest of the function, and everything the caller does with the returned string, only ever executes on a path where the read is known to have succeeded.

assessments.prompt: A function returns (int, error). The caller writes `value, _ := riskyCall()` and then immediately uses `value` in a calculation, without checking whether the call actually failed. What happens?
options: go build refuses to compile, because discarding a returned error with _ is treated as a compile error.
The program panics at runtime the moment the discarded error would have been non-nil.
Nothing stops it: execution continues normally, and value holds whatever riskyCall returned -- typically 0 (int's zero value) if it failed -- with no warning that anything went wrong.
Go automatically substitutes the last successfully returned value from a previous call instead of the zero value.
assessments.explanation: Assigning an error to the blank identifier `_` is completely legal and compiles without any complaint -- `_` is specifically exempt from Go's unused-variable check, precisely to allow deliberately discarding a value you don't need. If riskyCall failed, value simply holds whatever it returned alongside that discarded error, ordinarily the zero value for its type, and the program proceeds to use that value with zero indication anything went wrong. Option A is wrong -- there's no special compiler enforcement tied to discarding errors specifically. Option B is wrong -- panicking requires an explicit panic() call or a runtime fault; silently discarding an error does neither. Option D describes behavior Go has no mechanism for at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain why Go represents failure as an ordinary returned value rather than using exceptions, and what trade-off this creates for someone writing Go code every day.
assessments.modelAnswer: Go's designers deliberately chose to make failure paths as visible and ordinary as success paths. With exceptions, any line inside a try block can potentially throw, and often the only way to know which lines are actually capable of failing -- and what kind of failure -- is to read documentation or trace through the callee's source, because nothing about the calling code's own text signals it. Go instead puts the possibility of failure directly into a function's signature: a function that returns (Result, error) is telling every caller, right there in the type it exposes, 'this can fail, and here's the value you'll get to inspect if it does.' The error itself is just an ordinary value -- comparable, storable, passable to other functions, loggable -- with none of the special, invisible stack-unwinding behavior an exception has. The direct consequence is the idiomatic `if err != nil` check appearing after essentially every call that can fail, which is undeniably more repetitive, line for line, than wrapping a dozen risky calls in one try block with a single catch handling all of them together. Go's answer to that trade-off is that the repetition is buying something real: a reader can scan any function top to bottom and see, explicitly, every point where it might fail and exactly what happens at each one, without having to also mentally simulate an invisible control-flow tree of possible exceptions and where each one would eventually be caught. The visible cost is boilerplate; the payoff is that failure handling is never accidentally invisible or silently skipped by a reader (even though, as with the blank identifier, a writer can still choose to skip it on purpose).

concepts.title: Wrapping Errors: fmt.Errorf, %w, errors.Is, and errors.As
concepts.description: Idiomatic Go lets you add context to an error as it travels up the call stack while preserving the original error underneath it, and errors.Is / errors.As let callers test for that original error -- or extract a specific error type -- through any number of wrapping layers.
learningObjectives: Wrap an error with fmt.Errorf and the %w verb, and explain what %w preserves that %v does not.
Explain what an error chain is and how the Unwrap() error method links one error to the next.
Use errors.Is to check whether a specific sentinel error appears anywhere in a wrapped error chain.
Define a custom error type and use errors.As to extract it from a wrapped chain.
Explain why comparing a wrapped error to a sentinel with == fails even when errors.Is on the same values succeeds.
Identify the common mistake of using %v where %w was intended, and explain what silently breaks as a result.

sections.heading: Adding Context Without Losing the Original: %w
sections.body:
A low-level error message like `"permission denied"` is nearly meaningless by the time it bubbles up through several layers of calls, unless something adds context along the way -- *which* file, *which* operation was being attempted. The obvious approach is `fmt.Errorf("loading user config: %v", err)`, which produces a new error whose message is `"loading user config: permission denied"`. That reads fine to a human, but it has a real cost: `%v` flattens `err` into plain text and discards it as a distinct value -- the resulting error has absolutely no programmatic relationship to the original `err` anymore. Anything downstream that wanted to check 'was this ultimately a permission error?' can no longer do so except by fragile string matching on the message text.

`fmt.Errorf`'s `%w` verb solves exactly this: `fmt.Errorf("loading user config: %w", err)` produces a new error with the same human-readable message, but this new error also holds a real, retrievable reference to the original `err` underneath it, accessible via an `Unwrap() error` method the returned value carries automatically. Nothing about wrapping changes what gets printed by default -- `fmt.Println(wrapped)` still just shows the combined message -- the difference only shows up when code deliberately asks to look underneath, via `errors.Is` or `errors.As`, covered next.

sections.heading: Error Chains and the Unwrap Method
errors.Is: Checking for a Specific Error Anywhere in the Chain
errors.As: Extracting a Concrete Error Type
Common Mistakes: %v Instead of %w, Over-Wrapping, and Sentinel Visibility
sections.body:
The single most common mistake here is muscle memory: writing `fmt.Errorf("doing X: %v", err)` out of habit (or because that's what an older codebase does everywhere) when `%w` was actually intended. This compiles fine, runs fine, and even prints an identical message -- the failure is entirely silent and only shows up later, when some other code's `errors.Is` or `errors.As` check against that error mysteriously fails to find something that's clearly right there in the printed message. If a sentinel or typed error ever needs to be detectable by callers, every layer between where it's created and where it's checked must wrap with `%w`, not `%v` -- a single `%v` anywhere in that chain permanently severs the link at that point.

A second, subtler mistake is wrapping *and* logging the same error at every single layer it passes through, producing duplicate, redundant log entries for one underlying failure as it bubbles up through five function calls. The more common idiom is to wrap for context at each layer (cheap, and it costs nothing to add), but log only once, typically at the outermost boundary (an HTTP handler, a CLI's main function) where the full, fully-wrapped chain is available to log as one complete message. Finally, remember that a sentinel error is only checkable by other packages if it's exported (`ErrNotFound`, not `errNotFound`) -- an unexported sentinel can still be wrapped and returned, but no caller outside the defining package can ever write `errors.Is(err, thatSentinel)` against it, because they have no way to refer to it at all.

examples.title: A Three-Layer Wrap Chain, Unwound by errors.Is
examples.explanation: Three layers, each adding its own context with `%w`, produce one combined message that reads naturally top to bottom: `"starting app: loading settings: permission denied"`. Despite two layers of wrapping sitting between the original `ErrPermission` and the `err` that `main` actually holds, `errors.Is(err, ErrPermission)` still returns `true`, because it calls `Unwrap()` on `err` (getting the `loading settings: ...` error), then `Unwrap()` on *that* (getting `ErrPermission` itself), and finds a match at that second step. A plain `err == ErrPermission` would be `false` here -- `err`'s concrete value is the outermost wrapping error, not `ErrPermission` itself -- which is exactly the gap `errors.Is` exists to close.

examples.title: %v Silently Breaks the Chain That %w Would Have Preserved
examples.explanation: The printed message, `"calling API: request timed out"`, looks exactly the same as it would with `%w` -- there is no visible difference at the point of printing, which is precisely why this mistake is so easy to make and so easy to miss in review. But `%v` converts `err` into a plain string and discards the value itself; the error `callAPI` returns has no `Unwrap()` method pointing back at `ErrTimeout` at all. `errors.Is(err, ErrTimeout)` therefore returns `false`, even though `ErrTimeout` is unmistakably the root cause and is sitting right there in the message text -- `errors.Is` only ever walks a real chain of wrapped values; it never falls back to inspecting message strings.

examples.title: errors.As Extracting a Custom Error Type's Data
examples.explanation: `ValidationError` carries structured data (`Field`, `Value`) that a plain sentinel could never hold. After `handleRequest` wraps it once with `%w`, `err`'s concrete top-level type is the wrapping error from `fmt.Errorf`, not `*ValidationError` -- so a type assertion or switch on `err` directly would not find it. `errors.As(err, &ve)` walks the chain looking specifically for a `*ValidationError`, finds it one level down, and assigns it into `ve`, giving the calling code full access to `ve.Field` and `ve.Value` exactly as if it had received the original error directly, with no wrapping in the way at all.

misconceptions.description: fmt.Errorf("...: %v", err) and fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) do the same thing -- %w is just an alternative, slightly more modern-looking way to write %v for errors.
misconceptions.clarification: They print identically but behave completely differently underneath. `%v` converts `err` into a plain string and discards the value -- the resulting error has no relationship to the original one anymore. `%w` preserves a real, retrievable reference to `err` via an automatically-generated `Unwrap()` method, which is what lets `errors.Is` and `errors.As` find it later, no matter how many further layers wrap it afterward. Using `%v` where `%w` was intended compiles and runs with zero indication anything is wrong -- the mistake only surfaces later, as a mysterious false result from an `errors.Is`/`errors.As` check against an error that's clearly visible in the printed message.

misconceptions.description: errors.Is(err, target) is functionally the same as err == target, so it's only worth using out of habit or style preference.
misconceptions.clarification: They diverge the moment any wrapping is involved. `==` only ever compares the single value you're directly holding against target -- if err is a wrapping error sitting on top of target, that comparison is false. errors.Is instead walks the entire chain underneath err, calling Unwrap() repeatedly and checking each link, so it finds target correctly no matter how many layers of wrapping sit between the value you're holding and the one you're checking for. Reaching for errors.Is by default, even in code that isn't wrapped today, protects against a later refactor silently breaking a bare == check with no compiler error to flag it.

exercises.prompt: What does errors.Is return in each of these two cases, and why do they differ even though both print an identical-looking message?
hints: Both fmt.Println(errW) and fmt.Println(errV) print the exact same text -- the verb used doesn't affect the formatted message at all.
The difference is entirely in whether the resulting error value has a working Unwrap() method pointing back at ErrClosed.
errors.Is walks the chain via Unwrap -- if that chain was never formed in the first place (because %v was used), there's nothing for it to walk.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Both print 'send failed: connection closed' identically. errors.Is(errW, ErrClosed) is true, because %w created a real Unwrap chain back to ErrClosed. errors.Is(errV, ErrClosed) is false, because %v discarded the relationship entirely -- errV has no Unwrap() method leading back to ErrClosed, even though its message mentions the same text.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `withW` wraps `ErrClosed` with `%w`, so the error it returns carries a real `Unwrap()` method that leads back to `ErrClosed` -- `errors.Is(errW, ErrClosed)` walks that link and finds a match, returning `true`. `withV` wraps with `%v` instead, which flattens `ErrClosed` into plain text inside the new error's message and keeps no reference to the original value at all; the resulting error has no `Unwrap()` method pointing anywhere. Both `fmt.Println` calls print identical-looking text because the formatted message itself doesn't depend on which verb was used -- the divergence is entirely invisible until something actually calls `errors.Is` or `errors.As` and discovers that one chain exists and the other one simply never did.

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to detect a specific 'record locked' failure anywhere in the error chain and retry, but the retry branch never runs even when the underlying cause clearly is ErrRecordLocked. Find and fix the bug.
hints: saveChanges wraps the error with %w before returning it -- what does err in main actually hold: ErrRecordLocked itself, or a different, wrapping value?
A direct == comparison only matches if both sides are the literal same value -- does that hold once wrapping is involved?
Replace the == comparison with the function specifically designed to check for a sentinel anywhere inside a wrapped chain.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `saveChanges` wraps the original error with `%w`, so `err` in `main` is the *wrapping* error produced by `fmt.Errorf` -- a distinct value from `ErrRecordLocked` itself, even though `ErrRecordLocked` is exactly what caused the failure underneath it. `err == ErrRecordLocked` compares `err`'s actual concrete value against `ErrRecordLocked` and finds they're different values, so it's false, and the 'unrecoverable error' branch runs instead, even though this failure is clearly recoverable by retrying. Replacing the comparison with `errors.Is(err, ErrRecordLocked)` fixes it: `errors.Is` calls `Unwrap()` on `err`, finds `ErrRecordLocked` one level down, and correctly reports a match -- exactly the situation `errors.Is` exists to handle, since `==` alone cannot see through any wrapping layer at all.

assessments.prompt: A function does `return fmt.Errorf("step failed: %v", err)`. What is the concrete, observable consequence of using %v here instead of %w?
options: The program fails to compile, since %v cannot be used with an error-typed argument.
The printed message differs -- %v omits the underlying error's text entirely, while %w includes it.

The printed message is identical either way, but the returned error has no Unwrap() method leading back to the original err, so errors.Is/errors.As checks against it will fail to find that original error.
Using %v instead of %w causes fmt.Errorf to panic at runtime.
assessments.explanation: Both verbs produce the exact same formatted message text -- the difference is entirely about whether a real, walkable relationship to the original error is preserved. %w gives the returned error a genuine Unwrap() method pointing back at err; %v simply renders err's text into the new message and keeps no reference to it as a value. This means errors.Is and errors.As, which work by calling Unwrap() repeatedly, will never find the original error through a %v-created wrapper, even though its message is right there in the text. Option A and D are wrong -- %v with an error argument is completely valid and doesn't panic, it's simply the ordinary formatting verb applied to whatever String()/Error() the value produces. Option B is wrong -- both verbs include the wrapped error's text in the resulting message identically.

assessments.prompt: Explain how errors.Is and errors.As work in terms of the Unwrap() method, and why a codebase that wants sentinel errors or custom error types to remain detectable needs to be consistent about using %w rather than %v when adding context.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both errors.Is and errors.As operate on the idea of an error chain: any error value that implements Unwrap() error is a link pointing at whatever error it wraps, and that wrapped error might itself implement Unwrap(), forming a sequence of links down to some root-cause error with no further Unwrap() at all. errors.Is(err, target) walks this chain starting from err, calling Unwrap() repeatedly, comparing each link against target with == (or consulting a custom Is method if one is defined), and returns true the moment it finds a match anywhere along the way -- not just at the very top. errors.As(err, &target) does the same walk, but instead of testing equality against one known value, it looks for the first link in the chain whose concrete type matches target's type, and if found, assigns that error into target so the caller can read whatever extra data it carries. Both functions rely entirely on Unwrap() actually being present and correctly wired up at every layer between where an error originates and where it's eventually checked. fmt.Errorf's %w verb is what creates that Unwrap() link automatically when adding context to an error; %v does not -- it flattens the wrapped error into a plain string and discards the value, producing no Unwrap() method at all. If even one layer in a chain uses %v where %w was needed, the chain is permanently severed at exactly that point: any errors.Is or errors.As check performed above that point can never see past it down to the sentinel or typed error underneath, no matter how many other layers correctly used %w. Since a large codebase typically has error context added across many different functions and packages, staying consistent about %w whenever an error might later need to be identified by a caller is what keeps that identification actually working end to end, rather than silently breaking at whichever layer happened to use the wrong verb.

concepts.title: panic and recover: For Exceptional Conditions, Not Routine Errors
concepts.description: panic immediately unwinds the current goroutine's stack, running deferred calls as it goes, and recover can stop that unwind partway -- but idiomatic Go reserves both for truly exceptional, program-breaking situations, never as a substitute for returning an ordinary error.
learningObjectives: Explain what panic does to a goroutine's execution, and how deferred function calls run during the unwind.
Use recover inside a deferred function to stop a panic from crashing the whole program.
Explain why recover only has an effect when called directly inside a deferred function, and does nothing anywhere else.
Distinguish situations that idiomatically warrant a panic from those that should return an error instead.
Explain why a panic in one goroutine cannot be recovered by another goroutine, and why this makes unrecovered panics in background goroutines dangerous.
Convert a recovered panic into a returned error at a package's public API boundary.

sections.heading: What panic Actually Does
recover: Stopping the Unwind -- But Only From Inside a Deferred Function
Why Idiomatic Go Reserves panic for Truly Exceptional Situations
sections.body:
Everything said in this module about preferring explicit `error` returns over hidden control flow applies just as much to overusing `panic` as it does to exceptions in other languages -- a function that panics for an entirely routine, expected failure (a missing file, bad user input) is reintroducing exactly the invisible-failure-path problem Go's `error` convention exists to avoid, just under a different name. The idiomatic line Go draws: **use `panic` for situations that indicate a bug or a genuinely unrecoverable state -- something the calling code could not reasonably have anticipated and cannot sensibly continue past -- and return an `error` for anything a caller might reasonably want to detect and handle.**

This is exactly why the runtime itself only panics for things like an out-of-range slice index, a nil pointer dereference, or integer division by zero (note: *integer* -- float division by zero produces `+Inf` or `NaN`, not a panic) -- these represent a bug in the program's own logic, not an ordinary, expected outside-world failure. Compare this to `os.Open`, which returns an `error` rather than panicking when a file doesn't exist, precisely because 'the file isn't there' is a completely ordinary, expected outcome that well-written calling code should routinely check for and handle, not evidence that something is fundamentally broken. A useful rule of thumb: **panic if the program genuinely cannot proceed correctly from here; return an error if the caller might reasonably want to handle the situation and keep going.** Library code in particular should almost never panic for anything a caller could trigger through ordinary, valid-looking usage -- a panic escaping from a library into an application that merely called it with unusual (but not invalid) input is a poor experience for that application's own error handling, which had no signature-level warning that this call could abandon normal control flow entirely.

sections.heading: Panics Are Per-Goroutine: An Unrecovered One Kills the Entire Program
Turning a Recovered Panic Into an error at an API Boundary

examples.title: Deferred Cleanup Running in LIFO Order During a Panic
examples.explanation: The panic originates in `step3`, which immediately runs its own deferred `fmt.Println` before the unwind continues to `step2`, whose deferred print runs next, then to `step1`'s. Each function's deferred cleanup gets a chance to run -- in the order the panic passes through them, innermost first -- before the program finally terminates once the unwind reaches `main` with nothing having called `recover()` anywhere along the way. This is precisely why `defer` is the standard place to put cleanup logic (closing files, releasing locks, flushing buffers) in Go: it's guaranteed to run even when a function exits abnormally via panic, not just via an ordinary `return`.

examples.title: The Canonical recover Pattern with Named Returns
examples.explanation: `a / b` with `b == 0` triggers a genuine runtime panic (integer division by zero is one of the situations the Go runtime itself panics on), which immediately abandons the rest of `safeDivide`'s body -- the `return` statement on the line after never executes. The deferred closure runs anyway, because deferred calls always run regardless of how a function exits, and inside it `recover()` catches the in-progress panic, returning the panic value (a runtime error describing the divide-by-zero) instead of letting it continue unwinding. Because `result` and `err` are *named* return values, the deferred closure can assign directly to `err`, and that assignment is what the function actually returns to its caller -- `result` is left at its zero value, `0`, since the panicking line never completed. The second call, with a valid divisor, never panics at all, so `recover()` inside the (still-running, still-deferred) closure simply returns `nil`, and `err` is left untouched at its own zero value, `nil`.

examples.title: An Unrecovered Panic in a Goroutine Takes the Whole Program Down
examples.explanation: Worker 2 panics, but because `worker` itself has its own `defer`/`recover`, that panic never escapes past `worker`'s own stack frame -- it's caught right there, printed as a recovery message, and execution returns normally to the `for` loop in `main`, which goes on to run worker 3 without any disruption at all. Contrast this with the earlier `go func() { panic(...) }()` example that had no internal recover: had `worker` here omitted its `defer`/`recover`, a panic in worker 2 (called directly here, not even via `go`) would have propagated all the way up through `main` and crashed the whole program, never reaching worker 3 at all. The general lesson generalizes directly to goroutines launched with `go`: any goroutine that might panic on some input needs its own recover if a single bad case shouldn't be allowed to take the entire process down with it.

misconceptions.description: recover() stops an in-progress panic no matter where in the panicking function's call chain you call it, as long as it's called somewhere while that panic is happening.
misconceptions.clarification: recover() only has any effect when it's called directly by a function that was itself deferred -- calling it in ordinary, non-deferred code does absolutely nothing, even while a panic is actively unwinding through that exact function. And even inside a deferred function, it must be that specific deferred function's own body calling recover() directly; a function that the deferred function goes on to call does not count. Called anywhere outside this exact position, recover() simply returns nil and has zero effect on any panic that might currently be unwinding.

misconceptions.description: panic/recover is Go's version of try/catch, so it's a perfectly normal way to handle expected, routine failure conditions like a missing file or invalid user input, the same way exceptions are often used for those cases in other languages.
misconceptions.clarification: Idiomatic Go deliberately reserves panic for situations indicating a bug or a genuinely unrecoverable state -- not for ordinary, expected failure modes, which should return an error exactly as covered earlier in this module. Every idiomatic standard-library function that can fail in a routine way -- opening a file, parsing input, making a network call -- returns an error and never panics for that kind of failure, specifically because panicking for something a caller should reasonably expect and handle reintroduces the same invisible-control-flow problem that motivated Go's error-as-value convention in the first place. Using panic/recover as a general substitute for ordinary error returns fights against the language's own idioms and makes a function's real failure modes invisible from its signature.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, in what order, and does it crash?
hints: Multiple defers in the same function run in LIFO order -- last deferred runs first. Which of the two defers in risky was deferred second?
The recover() call is inside a deferred function -- does it successfully stop the panic here, or does the panic still escape risky entirely?
If recover() successfully catches the panic inside risky, does main() ever find out anything went wrong at all?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'risky: recovered from unexpected condition', then 'risky: deferred cleanup', then 'main: continuing normally' -- and it does not crash. The recover() defer runs first (LIFO order, deferred second) and successfully stops the panic, so the unwind never reaches past risky; the cleanup defer still runs afterward since all deferred calls run regardless, and main proceeds completely normally, with no way to even tell a panic happened unless it checks a return value (which this version doesn't provide).
exercises.solutionExplanation: `risky` defers two functions: the cleanup print (deferred first) and the recover closure (deferred second). When `panic("unexpected condition")` runs, deferred calls execute in LIFO order, so the recover closure runs first -- and because it's called directly inside a deferred function while the panic is actively unwinding through this exact point, `recover()` succeeds, returning the panic value and printing 'risky: recovered from unexpected condition'. This stops the unwind entirely: normal execution effectively resumes once `risky`'s remaining deferred calls finish, so the cleanup print still runs next ('risky: deferred cleanup', since deferred functions always run regardless of whether a panic occurred), and then `risky` returns completely normally to `main`, which proceeds to print its own line with no indication anything unusual happened -- because this version of `risky` has no return values at all, the fact that a panic was recovered is entirely invisible to the caller, illustrating why the earlier `safeDivide` example specifically threads the recovered value into a named `err` return instead of just printing it and moving on.

exercises.prompt: This server is supposed to keep handling incoming jobs even if one job's processing panics on bad data, but a single malformed job currently crashes the entire program and stops all remaining jobs from ever being processed. Find and fix the bug.
hints: processJob has no defer/recover of its own -- what happens to the whole program when a panic inside a goroutine is never recovered anywhere in that goroutine?
Recall that a panic only unwinds the goroutine it occurs in, but if it's never recovered before reaching that goroutine's entry point, the entire process terminates -- not just that one goroutine.

Add a deferred recover directly inside processJob (or inside the closure passed to go) so a panic while processing one job is contained to that job, instead of escaping and killing every other in-flight job.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `processJob` panics when it receives job 2's empty data, and since that goroutine has no `defer`/`recover` anywhere inside it, the panic unwinds all the way to the goroutine's entry point with nothing catching it -- which terminates the entire program immediately, taking down every other goroutine (including whichever jobs 1 or 3 hadn't finished processing yet) along with it, not just job 2. The fix adds a `defer func() { if r := recover(); r != nil { ... } }()` at the top of `processJob` itself, so a panic while processing any one job is caught and contained within that specific goroutine -- printing a failure message for that job alone, while every other goroutine continues running completely unaffected. This is the general pattern for any goroutine you launch yourself that might panic on bad input: give it its own recover, because nothing else in the program will protect it automatically the way net/http protects each request handler for you.

assessments.prompt: A background goroutine spawned with `go worker()` panics while processing one item, and worker itself has no defer/recover anywhere in its call chain. What happens?
options: Only that one goroutine silently stops; main and all other goroutines continue running unaffected.
The panic is automatically logged by the Go runtime and that goroutine is restarted from the beginning.

The panic unwinds worker's entire call stack with nothing to stop it, reaches the top of that goroutine, and terminates the whole program immediately -- every other goroutine, including main, is killed too.
recover() is called implicitly by the runtime at the goroutine's entry point, converting the panic into a silently discarded no-op.
assessments.explanation: A panic that is never recovered anywhere along its unwind path terminates the entire process the instant it reaches the top of whichever goroutine it occurred in -- this is true whether that goroutine is main or one spawned with go, and it takes every other goroutine down with it, not just the panicking one. Option A is wrong -- there's no such 'just stops that goroutine' behavior; an unrecovered panic is fatal to the whole program. Option B is wrong -- Go has no automatic goroutine-restart mechanism; a crashed process stays crashed until something external (an orchestrator, a supervisor) restarts it. Option D is wrong -- recover() is never called implicitly by the runtime; if you want a panic caught, you must write an explicit defer/recover yourself somewhere in that goroutine's call chain.

assessments.prompt: A developer new to Go asks: 'Why not just use panic everywhere instead of returning errors -- isn't it basically the same as throwing an exception, and wouldn't that be simpler?' Explain the idiomatic distinction Go draws between the two, and the specific danger of using panic for routine failures in concurrent code.
assessments.modelAnswer: Go deliberately separates two kinds of bad outcomes that many languages blur together under one exception mechanism. Ordinary, expected failures -- a file that doesn't exist, malformed user input, a network timeout -- are things a well-written caller should routinely anticipate and decide how to handle: retry, report to the user, fall back to a default. These are represented as ordinary error return values specifically so that every caller must at least receive that value and can inspect it inline, with the function's own signature honestly advertising that it can fail. panic is reserved for the other category: situations that indicate a bug in the program's own logic, or a state so broken that continuing normally is meaningless -- an index computed incorrectly and now out of range, a nil pointer that should never have been nil given the program's own invariants, a required startup dependency that simply isn't there. Using panic for the first category -- treating it as a general-purpose throw for routine failures -- reintroduces exactly the problem Go's error convention exists to avoid: a caller reading a function's signature has no way to know, without reading its full implementation, that it might abruptly abandon normal execution, and every caller now has to defensively wrap calls in recover just to behave the way a normal error check already would have. The danger becomes sharper in concurrent code specifically because panics are scoped per-goroutine but their consequence is not: a panic in one goroutine can only be recovered by a defer sitting somewhere in that same goroutine's own call chain, and if it isn't recovered there, the unwind doesn't just end that one goroutine quietly -- it terminates the entire program, killing every other goroutine, including main and any other in-flight, perfectly healthy work, along with it. A routine failure -- one bad request, one malformed job -- treated as a panic-worthy event in a goroutine with no recover of its own can therefore take down an entire running server over a single piece of ordinary bad input, which is a dramatically worse outcome than the equivalent error check would ever have produced.
